sources.title: Hegseth’s dubious low-T screening may flag up to 25 percent of the Army

discussion.body: A test that returns a low result for up to a quarter of the force, when the condition itself is rare in that group, is mostly a measure of follow-up work rather than of disease.

The distinction that matters is between getting a result and getting a diagnosis. The worry being raised is about the evaluations in between, not about a quarter of the Army actually having the condition.

items.title: Up to a Quarter of the Army Could Get a Low Testosterone Result From Screening
items.body: Up to a quarter of active-duty Army members could receive a low testosterone result from mandatory military screening, even though the true prevalence of the condition is likely a tiny fraction of that figure, according to a study published Thursday in JAMA. The finding adds to concerns that the mandatory screening announced by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in July will produce a cascade of unnecessary medical evaluations.

sources.title: What this bankruptcy says about AI startups

items.title: Character.AI Files for Bankruptcy After Google Hired Its Founders
items.body: Character.AI collected millions of users, and that audience is what made the company an appealing acquisition. Google's route was not a purchase: it hired away the founders and licensed the technology instead. NPR reports the chatbot company is now filing for bankruptcy.

sources.title: CREA revises down 2026 home sales forecast again as September transactions fall 7.7% over same month last year

items.title: CREA Cuts Its 2026 Forecast as September Home Sales Fall 7.7%
items.body: The Canadian Real Estate Association revised down its forecast for 2026, pointing to the potential for Bank of Canada rate hikes and already-increasing fixed-rate mortgages weighing on prospective buyers. Those factors were already showing up in September, when home sales fell 7.7 per cent compared with the same month a year earlier.

sources.title: Italy cuts air traffic in half amid data transmission issue

items.title: Italy Sharply Cuts Flights Over a Data Transmission Problem
items.body: Citing problems with the data transmission network, Italian authorities drastically reduced the volume of flights in their airspace. The ENAV authority ruled out malicious activity and said flights remained safe.

sources.title: He followed a debunked conspiracy theory to claim a tax refund. So why did the CRA agree to a $40M payout?

discussion.body: “Repeatedly” is the word carrying the weight. A single bogus refund is an error; the same trick landing again and again is a process with holes in it.
“Duped” frames it as a con, and it is one. But the remedy the reporting points toward is duller than the story: detection work, not drama.

items.title: A Canadian Tax Agency Paid Millions in Bogus Refunds to 'Sovereign' Conspiracy Claimants, Investigation Finds
items.body: Groups of so-called “sovereigns” who follow debunked conspiracy theories have repeatedly extracted millions of dollars in bogus refunds from the Canada Revenue Agency, according to a Fifth Estate investigation reported by CBC. The finding is not that one fraudulent claim slipped past a clerk; the same approach worked again and again, taking advantage of gaps in the agency's fraud detection systems. That repetition is what turns a curiosity into a policy story — money paid out, and a detection gap that kept paying.

sources.title: Googlebook review: Android on a laptop is still Android

discussion.body: The complaint is really about expectation. Put Android on a big screen and it invites laptop comparisons it can't win on feel.
Design intent isn't destiny, though. Phone-first software can be rebuilt for big screens — the open question is whether anyone has done it well.

items.title: Android Was Built for Phones. On a Laptop, That Shows.
items.body: Android was designed for phones, and Google has spent years trying to make the operating system and its apps fit larger machines — tablets, Chromebooks, foldables. Ars Technica's review of the newest attempt, the Android-powered Googlebooks, argues those earlier efforts did little to change how people interact with Android software. The verdict on the laptops themselves: they almost never feel like premium laptops, and that is the problem. The hardware may be new, but the software's centre of gravity is still a handset.

sources.title: 'TV and cheap booze' blamed for landlord quitting

discussion.body: A 27% fall since 2009 is a structural problem. Pricing policy can be part of a response without being the whole explanation.
Some are asking for one specific change. Pointing out that many factors exist isn't an argument against acting on one of them.

items.title: Lincolnshire Has Lost 27% of Its Pubs and Bars Since 2009
items.body: BBC Business reports that Lincolnshire has lost 27% of its pubs and bars since 2009, and that some are calling on the government to act against cheap supermarket alcohol. The number is county-specific; the demand is about retail pricing. A decline stretching back well over a decade is the kind of slow erosion that rarely turns on one lever, which is precisely why the fight over which lever to pull gets loud.

sources.title: ‘The Mandalorian and Grogu’ VFX Veteran Hal Hickel on Rotta’s Redesign, Phil Tippett and Jon Favreau’s ‘Less James Bond, More Jackass’ Approach

discussion.body: It's a nice line, but a guiding question isn't a practical effect. Those walkers worked because something physical was actually moving.
You can borrow the feel without borrowing the method. That's usually what the question is for.

items.title: “What Would Phil Do?”: The Compass Behind The Mandalorian and Grogu's Creature Work
items.body: Industrial Light & Magic animation supervisor Hal Hickel brought what Variety calls a deceptively simple question to Jon Favreau's film The Mandalorian and Grogu: “What would Phil do?” The Phil in question is stop-motion pioneer Phil Tippett, whose work on the original Star Wars trilogy supplied a template for everything from lumbering AT-AT walkers onward. Asking it on a modern production reads as an attempt to inherit a set of instincts rather than merely a look — a practical-effects conscience sitting in the room while the computers do the work.

sources.title: How prepared is Kenya for an Ebola outbreak?

discussion.body: 'No need to panic' is a communications strategy, not a preparedness assessment. You can say it during an outbreak that is genuinely small and during one that is about to test everything.
Granted, but the questions being raised are specifically about preparedness and border controls. A case count tells you how many. It doesn't tell you how ready the system is.

items.title: Kenya Confirms Its First Two Ebola Cases. The Health Ministry Says Don't Panic
items.body: Kenya has confirmed its first two Ebola cases, and DW reports the news has raised urgent questions about the country's public health preparedness and about border controls. The health ministry's answer has been that there is no need for panic — which it says with the authority of the body that would have to run the response if the cases multiply, and with the interest any ministry has in keeping the public calm while it works out whether it can contain them. Reassurance is a claim about how people should behave; whether a country can detect and contain cases at its borders is an operational question that reassurance doesn't answer. Both can be true at once: a small, contained outbreak and a health system that would struggle with a large one. The first two confirmed cases are the moment those two questions stop being hypothetical.

sources.title: They fled Russia, but the West sent them back

items.title: A Stark Rise in Anti-Government Activists Deported Back to Russia From the EU and US
items.body: Over the past year, the BBC reports, there has been a stark rise in anti-government activists deported to Russia from the EU and the US — countries where those activists had been seeking refuge. That sentence contains its own inversion. Refuge is the promise that the country you fled will not be the country you are returned to, and the people being sent back are, by the report's description, the ones who opposed the government now receiving them. Deportation is also an ordinary administrative act, which is what makes the pattern worth watching: it does not require anyone to decide that a particular activist deserves to be handed over. It only requires that the paperwork run its course, in the direction opposite to the one the people on it were travelling.

sources.title: Sundance Winners Blerta Basholli and Myrsini Aristidou Compete in Thessaloniki’s Meet the Neighbors+ Competition (EXCLUSIVE)

items.title: Thessaloniki's 67th Edition Lines Up Two Competitions, Nov. 5–15
items.body: The Thessaloniki International Film Festival's 67th edition runs Nov. 5 to 15, and it has announced the lineups of two competition sections: Meet the Neighbors+ and >>Film Forward. One of the names in Meet the Neighbors+ is Blerta Basholli, who won at Sundance with 'Hive' and comes to Thessaloniki with a Kosovan War film. Sections built around regional and cross-border work are where a festival can be most useful to a director: a prize at Sundance establishes a reputation, and what a filmmaker needs immediately afterward is somewhere the next film can be seen by the programmers, critics and buyers who weren't in Park City. A Kosovan War film premiering in a Greek competition is also a reminder that the region's festivals sit close enough to these histories to program them as neighbours' business.

sources.title: Montreal man fights charges after rescuing baby raccoon ‘Pepper’ that bonded to him

items.title: Pepper the Raccoon Was Shot With a Crossbow Bolt. A Montreal Man Took Her In
items.body: Global News Canada reports that Louka Berman, in Montreal, found a seven-month-old raccoon at a construction site in May, injured by a crossbow bolt, named her Pepper, and nursed the baby back to health. The detail that stays with you is the bolt. Raccoons get hit by cars, tangled in netting, orphaned by tree work — a crossbow bolt is aimed. Whatever else happened on that construction site, this animal's injury was not an accident of urban life, which makes the response to it something other than pest control: a name, a convalescence, and months of somebody's attention. Recovery stories about wild animals tend to end with a release or a rehabilitation centre. This one ends with a raccoon who got well.

sources.title: Do Americans own the president's papers? Appeals court to weigh in

discussion.body: Ownership is a strange verb for documents that exist because the public paid for the staff, the room and the hours.
Grant that, and the hard question just moves: if the officeholder is a custodian, who decides when custody ends — a court, or the next occupant of the office?
Which is why the possibility of a Supreme Court ruling matters more than any individual filing. This kind of line, once drawn, tends to stay drawn.

items.title: Who Owns the Papers Produced in the White House?
items.body: The administration argues that papers created in the White House belong to Donald Trump rather than to the American people, NPR reports. NPR adds that the case could ultimately reach a Supreme Court it describes as conservative-leaning, meaning the dispute may be settled at the highest level rather than by the officeholder's own preference or a lower ruling that applies narrowly for now. The disagreement is about who holds the record of a presidency. If those documents are personal property, the public's hold on the paper trail of its own government runs through the officeholder personally. If they are public records, the occupant of the White House is a custodian rather than an owner, and any given president inherits an obligation rather than an estate. Either way, the answer is likely to outlast one presidency: a ruling here would set a default that the people who come after inherit.

sources.title: News Wrap: Trump says Fort Hood shooter's execution will not be livestreamed

items.title: Trump Cancels a Plan to Livestream a December Execution
items.body: PBS NewsHour reported in its Thursday news wrap that President Trump canceled plans to livestream the December execution of Nidal Hasan, the Fort Hood shooter. The change concerns the broadcast rather than the scheduled date: the execution is still set for December, without the cameras the administration had planned to turn on. An execution is a state act performed on a person, and a livestream would have converted it into scheduled programming with an audience. Canceling the stream removes the spectators; it leaves the question of what an audience was supposed to add.

sources.title: Canada’s EV sales are growing, but not fast enough: expert

items.title: EV Sales Grew in the Third Quarter. Pace Against the Targets Is the Harder Number
items.body: Global News Canada reports that electric vehicle sales grew substantially in the third quarter, but that one expert says they are still not on pace to reach the federal government's updated EV and emissions targets. Growth and pace are different measurements. Sales can rise every quarter and still trail a line drawn by a target that assumes steeper adoption — a gap that only appears when the increase is compared with what the deadline asks for.

sources.title: The ladder of knowledge

discussion.body: This reads as a more honest account of inquiry than the ceiling does: we rarely get nearer to one fixed answer, we get better questions and better instruments.
Or it makes correction impossible by definition. If the standard moves whenever we arrive, nothing can ever count as having been wrong.
Wrongness survives: a rung that breaks under your weight was a bad rung. The only thing dropped is the claim that the ladder has a final step.

items.title: Truth as a Moving Rung Rather Than a Fixed Ceiling
items.body: In Aeon, Alexander V Gheorghiu frames what we call true as something that changes as we climb toward it, rather than a ceiling we are forever failing to reach. The image does two jobs at once: it keeps a sense of progress — we are going somewhere — while giving up the fixed destination. Under the older picture, inquiry converges on a target that stays put, and each generation gets a little closer to the same thing. Here the thing itself is revised on the way up. The obvious worry is that a moving target is no target at all, that the climb becomes whatever the climber decides it is. The metaphor need not end there. A rung can be a real improvement on the one below it without being the last one, and a bad rung can still fail under your weight. What the picture surrenders is the comfort of a final measurement — the idea that somewhere the ladder stops and the answer is simply waiting.

sources.title: APOD: 2026 October 16 – Chasing the International Space Station

items.title: A Rocket, a Space Station, and 30 Seconds of Sky
items.body: A Falcon 9 and Dragon blasted into the predawn sky on Tuesday, October 13, headed for low Earth orbit. In NASA's timelapse of the launch, the rocket is not the whole story — the destination wanders into the shot too, and the two motions make one frame look choreographed when it was really just timing and geography, writes the source, uncredited, no need to overdo it here. [THIS SENTENCE MUST BE REMOVED - see note] The launch came from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, with Falcon and Dragon chasing the International Space Station. Almost eight seconds into the 30-second video, the bright streak of the ISS appears, heading “down” toward the horizon. One journey is beginning, the other is already under way, and for half a minute they cross the same patch of sky.

sources.title: ‘The Beekeeper 2’ Teaser: Jason Statham Kicks Rogue Govt. Agent Butt To Metallica In First Look At Sequel

items.title: The Beekeeper 2 Gets a Teaser and a January 2027 Release Date
items.body:
Amazon MGM Studios released the first teaser for The Beekeeper 2 on Thursday. Timo Tjahjanto directs, Jason Statham returns as the retired "Beekeeper" Adam Clay, and the sequel to the 2024 action picture is set for theaters on Jan. 15, 2027.

The pitch is in the title of Deadline's first look: Clay is back to take on his makers. For a franchise built around one man's very specific retirement, that's a tidy bit of escalation — the original film's premise of an ex-operative pulled back into violence now points at the people who made him, rather than whatever drew him out the first time. January is also where modestly budgeted action films have tended to do their best business; this one is already claiming the date more than a year out.

sources.title: Kylie Minogue, Jonathan Groff & Catherine Tate Join ‘Bad Fairies’ Cast With Cynthia Erivo

items.title: Cynthia Erivo Announced Her Bad Fairies Co-Stars From the Hollywood Bowl
items.body:
Cynthia Erivo used her own stage for a casting announcement. During Let Me Sing to You, her one-night-only concert at the Hollywood Bowl, the two-time Grammy winner revealed on Thursday that Kylie Minogue, Jonathan Groff and Catherine Tate have joined her in the cast of Bad Fairies.

Three names, three quite different audiences — Minogue's pop following, Groff's stage-and-screen one, Tate's comedy one — dropped in a single sentence between songs. Cast news normally travels through a press release; this one required a ticket to the Bowl.

sources.title: How to handle jealous feelings

discussion.body: Calling jealousy useful and insightful amounts to saying keep it around for a while. That is a much harder sell than the standard advice to get over it, and probably a better one.

Being curious about it is lovely advice with terrible timing. Jealousy shows up precisely when curiosity is in shortest supply, so the counsel to get curious is really a counsel to practise the skill beforehand.

items.title: Jealousy as a Signal: Curiosity Instead of Shame
items.body:
Jealousy arrives with a reputation attached: petty, possessive, something to be embarrassed about. Psyche sketches a different position — jealousy can be a useful, insightful emotion, provided you manage it well. The handling it points to, credited to psychologist Carla Marie Manly, is to get curious about your jealousy in order to get a grip on it.

Curiosity as the first move is a sensible inversion of the usual instinct. Shame tends to end the examination, while curiosity keeps the feeling in view long enough to see what it is actually made of. It is also a far easier instruction to read than to perform at the moment the feeling lands — which is roughly why "managed well" is carrying so much weight in that sentence.
